note: Braces forbid narrowing conversions, which is why {} is the safer initialiser.
auto strips references and const; decltype(auto) preserves exactly what the expression is.
Members initialise in declaration order, not in the order you list them.
Read declarations right to left: const T* is a pointer to const, T* const is a const pointer.
constexpr may run at either time; consteval must run at compile time or fail to compile.
constinit guarantees static initialisation, killing the static initialisation order fiasco.
A stateless lambda deleter costs nothing extra if you name its type with decltype.
= delete removes an overload from the candidate set, which is stricter than making it private.
A scoped enum will not convert to int on its own, which is exactly why it is safer.
Catch by const reference; catching by value slices the derived exception down to its base.
explicit blocks the implicit conversion, so a Meters can never silently become an int.
A namespace alias shortens the call site without dragging every name into scope.
[=] copies, [&] aliases, and mutable makes the copy writable inside the body.
An immediately-invoked lambda lets you initialise a const with a multi-statement computation.
std::function type-erases and may heap-allocate; a template parameter keeps the lambda inline.
A noexcept move constructor is what lets vector reallocate by moving instead of copying.
std::move only casts to an rvalue; the moved-from object is valid but unspecified.
Define <=> and == and the compiler generates the other four relational operators.
operator() takes several indices; operator[] takes one, so a row view is the natural return.
Header guards stop double inclusion; inline lets a definition live in a header legally.
RAII runs the cleanup on every exit path, including the exception you forgot about.
The init-statement scopes a variable to the if or switch, which kills a whole class of leaks.
A reference must bind on creation and can never be reseated; a pointer can be null and moved.
Declaring any one of the five suppresses some of the others, so declare all five or none.
Two shared_ptrs pointing at each other never free; one side must be weak.
struct defaults to public, class to private. That difference is the whole language rule.
Structured bindings work on tuples, pairs, arrays and any struct with public members.
unique_ptr is move-only, so passing one by value transfers ownership visibly at the call site.
